summary:
Coahuila de Zaragoza stands under the national framework of Mexico, where Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that most states now operate administrative procedures for legal gender recognition while warning that implementation differs sharply between them, and where same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2009.

Coahuila is one of the states that has legislated. The 2018 Law on the Civil Registry of the State of Coahuila, articles 124 to 128, established an administrative procedure for recognition of self-identified gender identity; the Human Rights Watch state-by-state tracker of March 2025 records it among the 32 states with such a procedure and links the official gazette text of the reform. The bill reached the plenary of the Congress of Coahuila through proposals from several parliamentary groups and an initiative by former governor Rubén Moreira, and the dictamen was approved unanimously. It reformed article 133 of the Ley para la Familia de Coahuila de Zaragoza and created the Civil Registry law, whose article 2, fraction XI, defines gender identity as the personal and internal conviction.

The procedure is in working use. Ricardo Malacara, director of Coahuila's Civil Registry, stated in March 2023 that roughly 1,500 people had completed the legal gender-identity change before the Civil Registry from early 2019 to March 2023, in both directions, male to female and female to male.

Recognition on paper does not settle the wider risk environment. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021 and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, second only to Brazil's 100; a Guardian report of 24 July 2024 states that more than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022. On 18 July 2024 the legislature of Mexico City made transfemicide a crime carrying sentences of up to 70 years under the Paola Buenrostro law, named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and state authorities in 2024 to prevent and punish violence against trans people, to investigate LGBTI violations using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP of 22 November 2024 concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautions that this must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence. No Coahuila-specific incident or enforcement pattern appears in the sources assembled here, so visitor-facing risk in the state tracks the national baseline rather than a documented local pattern.
tangentialFactors:
Tabasco serves as the documented contrast case. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" of 6 March 2024 found that no administrative gender-recognition procedure exists there, that hate-motivation provisions are absent from its criminal code, that healthcare staff out patients by calling their legal names, and that the August 2023 killing of activist Karina Gómez remained unsolved. Delays and refusals in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police.

Violence intensified over the year to mid-2024. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, with the killings drawing street protests; Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. A trans woman was found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

Coahuila's 2018 enactment sits within a national expansion driven both by state legislatures and by Supreme Court rulings, so the trajectory across Mexico is toward wider recognition even where individual states lag.
localsOnly:
Approximately 3,500 transgender citizens held formal jobs at companies operating in Coahuila as of March 2023, according to Civil Registry director Ricardo Malacara, a figure that indicates the standing presence of trans residents in the state's workforce.

Residents complete the gender-identity change before the Civil Registry rather than through a court process, and the procedure has been available since early 2019 in both directions of transition.

Residents of Mexico City are covered by the Paola Buenrostro transfemicide statute of 18 July 2024, which provides sentences of up to 70 years; the statute does not extend to other states by its own terms.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Coahuila's criminal code contains hate-motivation or aggravating provisions for offences against trans people is not addressed in the sources assembled here and remains unresolved.

No Coahuila-specific killing, assault or enforcement failure involving a trans person appears in the inventory; the absence of such a record is not evidence that none occurs, and the state's actual violence figures are not sourced here.

Procedural detail for the Coahuila application itself, including any fee, waiting period, residency requirement or documentation burden, is not stated in the sources and remains unresolved.

The 1,500 figure for completed procedures is a March 2023 statement by a state official and has not been updated in the sources available; current volumes are not sourced.
